title: David and Jonathan (1 Samuel 18–20)
hook: a prince loves David as his own soul and warns him with arrows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Goliath, and a shepherd who took off the king's armor. Your line was not in borrowed armor.

On paper, these two should be rivals. One is Jonathan, King Saul's son and heir, a brave soldier in his own right. The other is David, who just killed Goliath. After the battle the women of Israel come out dancing with a song: Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. Saul hears it and something sours in him. From that day, the text says, he keeps a jealous eye on David. Jonathan is the one who stands to lose a kingdom. Instead, something else happens.
screen: `A PRINCE AND A SHEPHERD.` → `HIS THOUSANDS, DAVID'S TEN THOUSANDS.` → `A KING GROWS JEALOUS.`

segments.voice: It begins in one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit. The Hebrew verb means tied or bound together, the word for a knot. The two make a covenant, a solemn promise before God. And Jonathan seals it with a gesture: he takes off his own robe and gives it to David, then his armor, his sword, his bow and his belt. The heir to the throne hands the shepherd the clothes of a prince. Then Saul's jealousy turns murderous. He throws a spear at David and orders his servants to kill him. Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. He doesn't pretend the danger isn't real, and he abandons neither of them. He speaks up for David to his father's face, and his father hurls a spear at him too. Then comes the plan with the arrows. David hides in a field. Jonathan goes out to shoot with a boy. If he calls, the arrows are on this side of you, David is safe. If he calls, the arrows are beyond you, David must run. Jonathan shoots, and calls out: the arrow is beyond thee. The boy runs off with the arrows, knowing nothing. The two friends meet, kiss and weep, David most of all. They part with a promise: the Lord be between me and thee for ever. In the twelfth century, the English abbot Aelred of Rievaulx held these two up in his book on spiritual friendship: loyal when it costs a crown, honest when it's dangerous, and bound before God.
screen: `TWO SOULS KNIT TOGETHER.` · `A PRINCE GIVES AWAY HIS ROBE.` · `CAUGHT BETWEEN FATHER AND FRIEND.` · `THE ARROW IS BEYOND THEE.` · then, large: `HE LOVED HIM AS HIS OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a friend who stood by you when it cost them something, who spoke up for you in a room you weren't in, or stayed when leaving was easier. Picture their face, remember one specific thing they did, and let yourself feel how much it mattered. If you pray, thank God for them by name.
nefesh. Hebrew for soul, the whole living self: Jonathan loved David as his own nefesh, bound by a covenant that cost him a crown. Today's word.
Your line: knit to his soul. A friendship tied fast before God. Day four hundred two, in the books.

howItsDone: Catholics hear part of the David and Jonathan story at weekday Mass early in Ordinary Time, in one year of the two-year cycle (1 Samuel 18–19).

chat.meaning: Jonathan loved David as his own soul and bound himself by covenant, giving David his robe, even at the cost of a crown.

notes: Some modern readers interpret David and Jonathan's bond as romantic; the script follows the Church's traditional reading as covenant friendship and does not address the debate. Keeper to decide whether a sentence is needed.
Aelred of Rievaulx (De spiritali amicitia) discusses David and Jonathan as an example of true friendship; confirm.
Saul hurls a spear at Jonathan in 20:33 (Douay: took a spear to strike him); confirm.
The song 'Saul slew his thousands, and David his ten thousands' (18:7) is paraphrased.

Reviewer changed 'King Saul's oldest son, the crown prince' to 'King Saul's son and heir': the text never states Jonathan is the firstborn, though he is listed first (1 Samuel 14:49; 1 Chronicles 8:33) and treated as heir (20:31).

Audit (second sample): the 'knit, two threads into one cloth' image was built on the English word; the Hebrew (qashar) means tied or bound, so it now says that. Vague 'the Church has long honored this' replaced with the concrete Aelred reference, and howItsDone no longer repeats it. Confirm qashar in 18:1 and the weekday lectionary placement (Thursday, week 2, Year II).
